To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) EFL is able, but eEF1A cannot, spontaneously recharge with GMP-PNP in the absence of eEF1B; (ii) the G domain of EFL contains several sequence features that are absent from eEF1A; and (iii) the evolutionary history of eEF1α and eEF1B is consistent with a ratchet-like model of eEF1 replacement.

the eukaryote-specific elongation factor eEF1A has been lost independently in multiple lineagess and that the eEF1A paralog EFL is able, in the absence of the eEF1B subunit, to function as an elongation factor, which may explain the loss of eEFIA and eEFIBα in certain lineages.

(1) eEF1A has been independently replaced by EFL in several lineages; (2) eEF1B is not universally present; (3) eEF1α replacement is associated with eEF1B absence; (4) EFL is not dependent upon eEF1B; (5) EFL is likely able to spontaneously recharge; (6) EFL may have arisen through duplication of eEF1Bγ.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of a protein complex, which is essential for all life, and how it is maintained or lost.
the evolutionary dynamics of eEF1B and eEF1A.
the evolution of the elongation factor system in eukaryotic cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the loss of the guanine exchange factor eEF1B is the driving force behind eEF1A loss in multiple eukaryotes.
eEF1A and eEF1B have diverged to the point of being incompatible with one another, and EFL has been recruited to take their place.
the eEF1A/eEF1Bα system is an evolutionary ratchet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolutionary history of eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1A is characterized by the loss of eEFBα in some eukaryotic lineages and the subsequent loss of eEF-1A in others.
eEF1A has been lost independently in multiple eukaryotic lineages, and that eEF1B has also been lost in many of these lineages.
eEF1B has been lost in eukaryotic evolution, with the exception of the Archaea, which have eEF1B-like proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolutionary history of eEF1B and EFL is intimately linked to that of eEF1α.
the evolutionary trajectory of the translation apparatus is not necessarily a smooth progression towards a single, optimized state.
eEF1A loss is not a random process, but is instead driven by a series of steps that can lead to a stable, irreversible state.
